B15_00: Dividing animal cells, at the stage when the Golgi apparatus is broken down before mitosis so that it can be shared between the daughter cells. The breakdown is monitored as a checkpoint in some settings, so failure can block entry into division. It ensures both daughters inherit secretory capacity, linking cell cycle control to organelle inheritance.
B15_01: Peripheral nerves, where Schwann cells must maintain mature myelin long after first wrapping axons, to preserve fast nerve conduction. When this upkeep fails, demyelinating neuropathy follows, with slowed conduction, distal weakness and sensory loss, the clinical picture of several inherited Charcot-Marie-Tooth forms. It links nerve health to trophic support and to the survival of axons.
B15_02: Cells across tissues, concerning how the Golgi apparatus beside the nucleus is kept compact, positioned and connected. This organisation matters for directional secretion in polarised and migrating cells, for accurate sugar modification of secreted proteins, and for orderly breakdown and rebuilding of the Golgi during division. Disruption yields a fragmented Golgi, mistargeted secretion and altered surface glycan profiles.
B15_03: Cells undergoing programmed cell death, which must signal to macrophages and neighbouring cells that they are ready to be engulfed. Prompt clearance matters because uncleared dead cells leak their contents and provoke autoimmunity and inflammation. The process links death signals delivered by immune cells to corpse removal, and a related surface change in activated platelets supports blood clotting.
B15_04: Cell surface organisation in many cell types, especially endothelium and muscle, concerning specialised membrane platforms where signalling is initiated and certain invaginations form. These platforms support uptake of material and mechanosensing. Their loss causes muscular dystrophy and cardiomyopathy and disturbs vascular tone and lipid handling, coordinating surface organisation with cell shape and adhesion.
B15_05: Dividing cells at the end of mitosis, when each daughter must rebuild a sealed nucleus around its chromosomes. Without this step the nucleus stays leaky and chromosome fragments can be stranded outside it. The consequences, micronuclei and genome damage, are associated with chromosomal instability in cancer, so this step safeguards genome integrity in proliferating tissues.
B15_06: Dividing cells, concerning both the breakdown and rebuilding of the nuclear envelope around each daughter genome. Reforming a sealed envelope restores the separation of nucleus and cytoplasm and lets normal nuclear function resume. Failure leaves persistent holes, micronuclei and genome damage, threatening genome stability in proliferating tissues and contributing to cancer-associated chromosomal instability.
B15_07: Dividing cells, after the Golgi has been fragmented and shared between daughters, when it is rebuilt into functional stacks. This lets each daughter resume secretion, sugar modification of proteins and polarised traffic without building the organelle from scratch. Its disruption is linked to Cohen syndrome, a developmental disorder with neutropenia and intellectual disability, and to cell polarity and stress responses.
B15_08: All eukaryotic cells, concerning delivery of a class of membrane proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum after they are made. These proteins include vesicle fusion machinery, electron-transfer components and many cell-death regulators, so their correct placement supports membrane traffic, metabolism and apoptosis. Loss of this delivery system broadly destabilises membrane protein production, with developmental and neurological consequences.
B15_09: Cells making transporters, channels and receptors that cross the membrane many times, concerning their correct insertion and orientation in the endoplasmic reticulum. Because such proteins dominate the secretory and ion-transport machinery, defects cause misfolding, disturbed ion handling and endoplasmic reticulum stress. In humans, loss of one component produces a developmental syndrome with skeletal and craniofacial anomalies.
B15_10: Neurons and other cells, concerning the maturation, positioning and sorting functions of endosomes that route internalised material toward degradation, recycling or self-digestion. Several factors involved are mutated in Parkinson disease and related neurodegeneration, reflecting how strongly neurons depend on accurate endosomal maturation and sorting for synaptic vesicle recycling and protein turnover.
B15_11: Cells throughout the body, especially neurons with very long axons, concerning the network of narrow tubules forming the peripheral endoplasmic reticulum. This network makes contacts with other organelles and extends along axons to reach distant synapses. Mutations in several components cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, linking the network's shape to the survival of long corticospinal motor axons.
B15_12: Cardiac and skeletal muscle cells, concerning the inward tubular extensions of the surface membrane that carry electrical excitation deep into each fibre. This network allows excitation to trigger uniform, synchronous contraction. When it fragments or detaches, as in heart failure and several myopathies, contraction becomes slow, uneven and weak, making it an important feature of cardiac and muscle disease.
B15_13: Cells of secretory tissues and indeed all eukaryotic cells, concerning the arrival and merging of transport vesicles with the Golgi apparatus. This step sustains secretion, sugar modification of proteins and the flow of newly made proteins toward the cell surface. Its loss collapses Golgi structure and blocks the secretory pathway, impairing every function that depends on secreted and surface proteins.
B15_14: Blood platelets and dying or stressed cells, concerning loss of the normal asymmetric arrangement of membrane lipids when cells are activated. In platelets this creates the procoagulant surface needed for clotting, and its failure causes Scott syndrome, a bleeding disorder. The process also marks dying cells for engulfment and supports shedding of microvesicles, linking cell activation to coagulation and clearance.
B15_15: The outermost layer of the skin, where keratinocytes terminally differentiate and form a tough shell that seals the stratum corneum. This barrier keeps water in and microbes and allergens out. Defective formation underlies ichthyosis and the compromised barrier of atopic dermatitis, so the process is central to skin health and to allergic sensitisation through the skin.
B15_16: Cells throughout the body, concerning where the endoplasmic reticulum is positioned relative to the plasma membrane and other organelles. These positions determine where lipid exchange and ion signalling occur. Loss of this organisation disturbs cellular ion stores and lipid balance, and one inherited mutation causes a familial motor neuron disease, linking organelle placement to neuronal survival.
B15_17: Cells that recycle their surface receptors and transporters, concerning the shaping of carriers that return them from endosomes to the surface or the Golgi. Without this step, those proteins are degraded instead of reused, so surface levels of nutrient receptors, adhesion molecules and signalling receptors fall. It supports polarised recycling in epithelial and other polarised cells.
B15_18: All eukaryotic cells, concerning how membrane proteins acquire their correct orientation as they are made in the endoplasmic reticulum. Failure leaves weakly anchored proteins unable to settle in the membrane, so they are destroyed instead of folded. Loss reduces levels of many receptors, transporters and channels, affecting secretory capacity and protein quality control throughout tissues.
B15_19: Dividing animal cells undergoing open mitosis, in which the nuclear envelope must be broken down so that the division apparatus can reach the chromosomes. Without it, chromosome capture and separation fail and the cell cannot complete division. The step is coupled to rebuilding the nucleus in daughter cells and is essential for proliferation in growing and renewing tissues.
B15_20: Brain and spinal cord white matter, where oligodendrocytes must continually renew mature myelin long after first wrapping axons. This upkeep keeps axons insulated, conduction fast and fibres metabolically supported. Its failure produces late-onset demyelination, axonal degeneration and leukodystrophy-like disease, including forms of hereditary spastic paraplegia, rather than a defect of initial development.
B15_21: Cells throughout the body, especially neurons with long axons and the developing brain and eye, concerning how much tubular endoplasmic reticulum network a cell builds. Network shape governs contacts between organelles and membrane traffic. Loss of these activities in humans causes hereditary spastic paraplegia and Warburg micro syndrome, a disorder with microcephaly, eye malformations and severe developmental delay.
B15_22: Tissues where cells must attach to and remodel their surrounding matrix, concerning how much of the adhesion receptor apparatus cells produce. Raising it strengthens attachment and migration, which is relevant to tissue fibrosis and wound repair, epithelial and endothelial adhesion, and tumour cell invasion, where increased adhesion changes matrix engagement and motility. Hormonal status also influences this control.
B15_23: Mammalian cells, where the Golgi stacks are linked into a single ribbon near the centre of the cell. This organisation supports orderly secretion, uniform sugar modification of secreted and surface proteins, and secretion toward one face of polarised or migrating cells; it is deliberately dismantled at division. Ribbon fragmentation is a recurring feature of neurodegenerative disease and of stressed cells.
B15_24: Cells responding to growth factors and cytokines, concerning how late endosomes become sorting stations that send surface receptors for destruction or release them as exosomes. This is how activated receptors are permanently switched off; failure leaves them signalling, contributing to tumour growth and neurodegeneration. The same machinery serves cell division, nuclear resealing and viral budding, which viruses such as HIV exploit.
B15_25: Cells throughout the body, concerning how readily membranes are pulled into narrow tubes during uptake, organelle remodelling and vesicle release. This balance determines whether carriers pinch off or persist, shaping endosomal traffic, self-digestion and uptake of surface receptors. It is relevant to nutrient uptake, signalling and inherited disorders of membrane traffic such as centronuclear myopathy.
B15_26: Mechanically stressed tissues such as skeletal muscle, whose cells routinely tear their surface membrane during contraction and must reseal within seconds to survive. The concern is how fast and how completely that repair proceeds, and when damage is too great the response shifts cells toward death. Impaired resealing underlies muscular dystrophies, linking membrane repair to muscle integrity and degeneration.
B15_27: Cells throughout the body and especially neurons, concerning formation of the tubular network of the peripheral endoplasmic reticulum, which contacts other organelles and follows cells as they extend processes. Mutations in several components cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, implying that long motor axons depend particularly on a properly shaped endoplasmic reticulum for their survival.
B15_28: Cells throughout the body, concerning the joining of endoplasmic reticulum tubules so the network stays continuous, allowing its contents to spread throughout the cell and permitting remodelling during growth and after division. Defects cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and hereditary sensory neuropathy, linking network continuity to the maintenance of long motor and sensory axons.
B15_29: Cells taking up material from their surroundings, concerning the acidification of endosomes as they mature. Acidity frees internalised cargo, supports nutrient uptake, receptor recycling and degradation, and is exploited by viruses and toxins to enter cells. Failure disrupts sorting and degradation, and the same acidification supports the secretory and killing granules of cytotoxic lymphocytes, linking it to immune function.
